text.p: France's increasingly confident opposition left ridiculed the "odd couple" cast in the role of saviours of the centre-right on Thursday while the conservative government struggled to avert defeat in Sunday's parliamentary election.

Outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe conceded in a radio interview the Socialist-led opposition could win the decisive runoff and pleaded with his backers to campaign "with a bit more fire and passion" in the dying days of the race.

Even some senior centrists in the ruling coalition voiced dismay at a tandem of socially-minded National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin and free-marketeer Alain Madelin, thrust into the limelight in a last-ditch unity gamble.

"This is an impossible couple of the least social and the most anti-European," Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin said. Seguin is a recent convert to a single European currency, former finance minister Madelin wants big cuts in the state's role.

"It's too late to impress people with a dance between the carp and the rabbit," said left-winger Jean-Pierre Chevenement, campaigning with Jospin in Paris. "This is a final illusion, a farewell waltz."
Francois Leotard, head of the ruling Gaullists' centrist UDF allies , called the team a pie containing "a liberal skylark and a big piece of Socialist horsemeat".
He said the right had ended up with the incongrous duo because it had never made its mind up what policy to pursue.

Seguin was right-wing voters' favourite for premier even before Juppe said he would resign next week after the left mauled the right on the May 25 first round. Madelin, the nearest France comes to a Thatcherite, could become finance minister.
Stocks in the Paris bourse's CAC index closed 0.15 percent lower on Thursday, still jittery after the index plunged 3.6 percent on Wednesday on speculation about a left-wing win.
Prices offered by bookmaker City Index Ltd suggested that the Socialists, Communists and other leftists would win about 300 seats, a comfortable majority in the 577-member Assembly.
Before a recent flurry of private opinion polls this week, most money was on the centre-right keeping a slim majority in the Assembly where it held a 464-seat stranglehold.
Jospin, sounding increasingly confident of winning, started talking about his first moves in office, putting stress on moves to combat record 12.8 percent unemployment.
If elected, he form a tight pluralistic cabinet reflecting the components of his alliance with Communists and Greens, he told the newspaper Sud Ouest.

He said his first move would be to call talks next month on cuts in the working week to create jobs, and controlled wage rises to help consumers and revive the economy. He would later present a budget focused on jobs, education and research.

Jospin aides said his third move would be to discuss with European partners the conditions he has set to join the euro currency, while reaffirming that he favoured European economic and monetary union.

Conservative leaders rained warnings on voters not to force President Jacques Chirac to "cohabit" with a left-wing prime minister. Chirac dissolved the Assembly last month gambling that his allies would cruise to re-election.
The president said he needed a "new elan" to lead France to a single European currency, but the centre-right has gradually drifted away from the strict conditions for monetary union.

Former budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy, one of the right's senior spokesman, said on Thursday there was a consensus in the coalition that the single currency should "not be rejected because we are not exactly at 3.0 percent" in the ratio of public deficits to gross domestic product.
Juppe said nothing good would come of a left-wing forcing Chirac to share power for five years in a relationship with a left-wing government that would be "inevitably antagonistic."

He accused the Socialists of promising the moon with pledges of creating 700,000 youth jobs and cutting the working week to 35 hours from 39. But Juppe's own promises of a war on jobs two years ago went nowhere -- unemployment is up.
Ex-premier Edouard Balladur, who shared power with the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand for two years, said everything should be done to avoid cohabitation again.
Leotard ridiculed a situation in which the president would say "yes" to the European single currency, the prime minister would say "maybe" and communist ministers would say "no".
